title: Spatializing Crisis and Constructing Governmental Competence: A Multimodal Analysis of BBC News and CNA’s Early COVID-19 YouTube Coverage
content: Early news coverage helps make unfamiliar health threats intelligible, yet less is known about how language and imagery jointly organize crisis meanings in platform-distributed broadcast journalism. This study examines how the early COVID-19 outbreak was constructed in 66 BBC News and 195 CNA YouTube videos published between 20 January and 12 March 2020 and identified through the outlets’ designated playlists. Using inductive thematic analysis, the study coded the corpus qualitatively and interpreted recurring linguistic and visual patterns through discourse and multimodal analysis. Within the selected BBC News coverage, descriptions and images of enclosure, disrupted mobility, and repatriation represented Wuhan as an immobilized crisis space; narratives of hiding and escape associated restricted movement with vulnerability and departure with relative safety. Within the selected CNA coverage, evaluative language, quantification, and authoritative sourcing constructed the outbreak as severe, while inter-agency coordination, visible leadership, procedures, and regulatory enforcement represented it as administratively manageable and positioned public authorities as capable organizers of the response. These higher-order organizing logics are conceptualized as spatialization and governability. Governmental competence denotes an institutional identity constructed within CNA’s coverage, not an independent assessment of Singapore’s response. By showing how recurring verbal and visual resources cohered into outlet-specific crisis narratives, the study contributes an analytically transferable framework for multimodal crisis and health communication research. The findings remain limited to the two examined corpora and the defined period.
